Trazarlas enteras cumple las técnicas avanzadas aisladas por medición, la tabla de tokens, costo y la figura y el criterio de costo sin tocar el compromiso de privacidad.

aic:110663.texto:
For this frenetic scene, Eugène Delacroix took inspiration from “The Giaour,” a poem in a popular series of romantic tales by the celebrated English poet Lord Byron. Giaour is a derogatory Turkish word for a Christian or non-Muslim applied here to the warrior at left clad in swirling white drapery. Amid a violent struggle, the Giaour is avenging the death of his lover at the hands of his opponent. Delacroix mirrored the two central figures and their horses as the Giaour is about to strike the fatal blow against the faceless Turk Hassan. The artist’s mastery of color is exemplified by his use of shimmering primary hues, while the loose handling of paint creates the sense of dynamism Delacroix was so capable of executing.
This painting reflects Delacroix’s sustained engagement with Orientalism, the artistic representation of non-European people and places, especially North Africa, Asia, and the Middle East. Delacroix was among the first European artists to travel to Africa when he visited Morocco in 1832, shortly after he completed this painting. Widespread in the nineteenth century, Orientalism was regularly leveraged to reinforce French colonial enterprises through often fantastical, violent, or erotic depictions of the customs and cultures of faraway locales.
aic:110663.title: The Combat of the Giaour and Hassan

aic:15468.texto:
As a model of Christian knighthood, Saint George was a popular figure in the Middle Ages. Artists most frequently represented the episode from his legend in which he slays a dragon and rescues a beautiful princess set to be sacrificed to the beast. The Catalan painter Bernat Martorell included a wealth of detail in his version of the story. Animal and human bones litter the foreground. Lizards—or perhaps baby dragons—crawl around the opening of the dragon’s cave. The princess’s parents and throngs of onlookers crowd the town’s battlements to view the action. Martorell enlivened the physical surface of the painting as well: He richly modeled George’s halo and armor and the scaly body of the dragon with raised gesso decoration, and he gave granular texture to the depiction of the sandy foreground.
Saint George and the Dragon was the central panel of an altarpiece devoted to the saint and was originally surrounded by four smaller narrative panels showing his martyrdom (now in the Musée du Louvre, Paris). Martorell probably painted the altarpiece for the chapel of the Barcelona palace of the government of Catalonia, a region whose patron is Saint George.
aic:15468.title: Saint George and the Dragon

aic:15468.texto: Probably commissioned for the chapel of Saint George, Palau de la Generalitat, Barcelona [Sobré in Wolff 2008]; Don Francesc de Sales de Rocabruna i Jordà, Baron of Albi, by 1867, died 1874 [lent by him to Barcelona 1867, along with the four lateral panels now in the Louvre, Paris, and a painting of the Virgin, probably the painting now in the Philadelphia Museum of Art]; when his estate was divided between his sister Maria Josepa de Rocabruna i Jordà (d. 1890) and his widow Josepa de Rocabruna i Pascual (died 1884), Saint George and the Dragon is likely to have passed to his widow, since two of her three executors correspond to the executors mentioned in the confused account of the painting’s sale in Sanpere y Miquel 1906, vol. 1, p. 195, vol. 2, p. 275 [see Macías and Cornudella 2011-2012, pp. 21-22 for the family relationships and likely transmission]. Don José Ferrer-Vidal i Soler, Barcelona, by 1906, until 1917 [Sanpere y Miquel 1906, vol. 1, p. 194, see also Macías and Cornudella 2012, p. 22 and Sánchez Sauleda 2014, p. 429]; sold by him to Charles Deering, Marycel, Sitges, near Barcelona, and Chicago, in 1917 [see Sánchez Sauleda 2014]; the painting was placed on loan at the Art Institute in 1921; loan agreement, Nov. 18, 1921, Art Institute Archives]; given to his daughters, Marion Deering McCormick and Barbara Deering Danielson, 1924 [Art Institute Archives]; given by them to the Art Institute, 1933.
aic:15468.title: Saint George and the Dragon

aic:81505.texto: In 1832 Eugène Delacroix joined a diplomatic envoy to French-colonized Algeria. The sights and experiences from this six-month journey fueled the rest of his career, lending his canvases an illusion of accuracy that his less-traveled competitors lacked. The artist expressed in his journals from abroad his admiration for Arab culture, even characterizing it as superior to that of post-revolutionary France. Nevertheless, in paintings like this he catered to violent European fantasies about the Arab world. Having never witnessed a lion hunt, Delacroix skillfully synthesized studies of landscapes, Islamic costume, and zoo animals to bring this narrative to life with theatrical intensity.
aic:81505.title: Lion Hunt

aic:81505.texto: Possibly sold from the artist to Vaisse for 2,500 francs [this and the following information according to Johnson 1989]. Austin Robertson, New York; his estate sale, New York, American Art Association, April 7, 1892, lot 147 (ill.); sold for 13,000 francs to Mr. and Mrs. Potter Palmer, Chicago; bequeathed to the Art Institute, 1922.

cma:150082.texto: This painting focuses upon the struggle between good and evil for the soul of a young woman. Looking out at the viewer, she is shown in the upper center of the composition, immediately below an angel and directly above Satan. At the upper right Saint Michael—holding scales for weighing the goodness of souls—admits the blessed to Heaven. Below, the Damned struggle to avoid the fiery pits of Hell and the demons that will torment them for eternity. At the time Tassaert painted this work, France was undergoing considerable political upheaval. In 1848, the country was wracked by a civil war between royalist and republican forces. Tassaert himself believed strongly in the Republic, and probably intended the young woman—caught between the sensual, worldly temptations of royalist excesses and the noble, pure ideals of the Republic—to personify the country of France.
cma:150082.title: Heaven and Hell

cma:97169.texto: This painting is a copy of a print by Jan Harmensz Muller (Dutch, 1571–1628), originally based on a painting by Spranger. Spranger often used the iconography of Ceres and Bacchus, two important agricultural deities. Muller's print has the Latin inscription Sine Cerere et Bacchio friget Venus, which translates to "without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus grows cold." The motto indicates that Love, represented by Venus, is impossible without the nourishment of food and drink, as the deities of grain and wine walk hand in hand.
cma:97169.title: Ceres and Bacchus

invariante_et6.nota: Las **dos** direcciones son error de corrida (la forma declarada del artefacto). la precondición declarada mira la cadena **antes** de correr y la degradación registrada registra lo que falló; sin la forma declarada del artefacto, una etapa muda pasa por omisión legítima. Lo verifica el ejecutor al cerrar y lo vuelve a verificar `MétricasDeRanking` al leer (la regla de qué corridas agregan a la tabla).

latencia.nota: 🔑 **Esto acota el recuadro ⚠️ de la observabilidad.** Ahí se declaraba que *las etapas puras no tienen span* —el `Fusionador` y el `RenderizadorDeSalida` no llaman a ningún puerto— y que por lo tanto *prometer latencia por etapa sobre-promete*. Instrumentando en el **`EjecutorDeEtapas`**, que es el lugar que ese mismo recuadro señala, **sí hay latencia para las ocho**. la latencia por etapa deja de estar sobre-prometido. **Va reportado.**

nota_de_identidad: Clase 2 (la tabla de identidades): *registro de una ejecución*. La identidad fija **las entradas, no la salida** —una salida no determinista con la misma entrada es el dato que el muestreo fijado, registrado y con su variabilidad medida mide—, así que lleva **ordinal** y la regla de que un id determina su contenido no aplica. El ordinal se **reserva** creando el directorio de forma exclusiva: `1 + n` es un *leer, después escribir* y el barrido es paralelo.
nota_de_la_tabla: degradación/la regla de qué corridas agregan a la tabla: una corrida con degradación **no planificada** no agrega a la tabla C0–C4 —*una C4 que degradó en silencio entraría etiquetada como C4 comportándose como C3*— y una con degradación **planificada** tampoco: es el criterio de respuesta garantizada y se reporta aparte. Una etapa **ausente por configuración** no degrada: no corre, y por eso C0–C3 sí agregan.
nota_de_ob2: *Los tokens se **persisten en el artefacto de corrida**, no solo en LangSmith* (los tokens en el artefacto de corrida): si el servicio se cae, se pierde la herramienta de debugging, **no los números** que la tabla de tokens, costo y la figura y el criterio de costo publican. Y el árbol declara qué se trazó y qué no, que es el registro de decisiones hecho artefacto.

etapas.politica: no degrada: es el piso (la asimetría del piso de recuperación). Si falla, la consulta falla.

etapas.nota: la evidencia copiada por valor es la **identidad** sobre `license`, `source_url`, `texto`, `title` y `artist`: esta pieza devuelve `Fragmento`s completos y no dicts proyectados, así que *no hay proyección* que pueda olvidar una columna. Y `media_license` **no está en el tipo** (la licencia de imagen y metadata), así que el renderizador no puede leerlo mal.
etapas.politica: evidencia vacía para la obra afectada → el generador **abstiene** por esa obra (degradación). La obra sale igual, con su metadata y su link.

binding.nota: el binding como único camino al puerto: el binding es el **único camino al puerto** y el prompt es parte de su identidad, no un argumento. la atribución de cada llamada a su rol: la llamada se atribuye a `rol`, no al nombre de la etapa. El `base_url` **no** es ingrediente: sale de `[proveedor]`.

Un `dato` sin `refs`, una `observacion` con `refs` y una `ref` numérica no se pueden construir (`dominio/explicacion.py`). Lo que el prompt pide es la calidad; lo que el tipo garantiza es la forma.

pipeline.nota: **Las cinco configuraciones son subsecuencias de una sola cadena** (la clausura de la etapa, la ablación por configuración), no cinco pipelines. la precondición declarada las rechaza antes de correr por dos caminos: precondiciones insatisfechas, y una cadena que no coincide con la fila que `[consulta] configuracion` dice ser.
